blocks.text: ما ناح قمري الحمام المطوق [mā nāḥa qumrī al-ḥamām al-muṭawwaq] [col. 52] [II, 591] How the wood pigeon, the ring-necked dove, laments. Alkazuinius: ان بيض القماري يجعل تحت الفواخت وبيض الفواخت يجعل تحت القماري كلاهما ينغقان قماري كافورية مطوقة [inna bayḍ al-qamārī yujʿal taḥt al-fawākhit wa-bayḍ al-fawākhit yujʿal taḥt al-qamārī kilāhumā yanghaqān qamārī kāfūriyya muṭawwaqa] Whether the eggs of the wood pigeon are placed under the phabe, or the eggs of the phabe under the wood pigeon, nothing will be hatched from them but camphor-coloured, ring-necked wood pigeons. The other derivation is taken from the Arabic language, in which الحر [al-ḥurr] alhorro is the young of a dove or of a turtledove, and ساق حر [sāq ḥurr] sako horrin is the wood pigeon. Alcamus: الحر فرخ الحمامة [al-ḥurr farkh al-ḥamāma] Alhorro, the young of a dove; Giggeius adds, or of a turtledove. ساق حر ذكر القماري [sāq ḥurr dhakar al-qamārī] Sako horrin, the male of the wood pigeons. And elsewhere: الورشان طاير وهو ساق حر لحمه اخف من الحمام [al-warashān ṭāyir wa-huwa sāq ḥurr laḥmuhu akhaff min al-ḥamām] Alvvarsen, a bird, namely sako horrin, whose flesh is lighter than that of the dove. The Arabs say it is so called from its call. Ibn Sida: سمي القماري ساق حر لصوته فانه يقول ساق حر ساق حر [summiya al-qamārī sāq ḥurr li-ṣawtihi fa-innahu yaqūl sāq ḥurr sāq ḥurr] The wood pigeon is called sako horrin on account of its call, because it says Sako horrin, Sako horrin. In the same way another species of wood pigeon, قطا [qaṭā] kata or katta, is also thought to be named from its call. Damir: سميت بحكاية صوته [summiyat bi-ḥikāyat ṣawtihi] It has its name from the likeness of its call. For, they say, when it comes to its young, bringing water in its crop, صاحت قطا قطا [ṣāḥat qaṭā qaṭā] it cries Katta, Katta. But this is pure invention. For قطا [qaṭā] katta is bent from the Greek name of the wood pigeon, φάττα [phatta]. The Arabs often change Greek φ and π into Kaph, because among them ف Phe and ق Kaph have the same shape and differ only in the dots, Phe having a single one and Kaph a double. Accordingly in Avicenna قوقي [qūqī] kauke are seals. In the Arabic Dioscorides قوطوما [qūṭūmā] is φύτευμα [phyteuma], قوقي [qūqī] keuke is πεύκη [peukē], قرقسيون [qarqasiyūn] karkesion is καρπήσιον [karpēsion], قوقس البحر [qūqas al-baḥr] kukos albahri is φύκος θαλάσσιον [phykos thalassion]. That this is not a slip of the copyists but of the authors is clear from the fact that these words are arranged in alphabetical order and are listed under the letter Kaph. Thus, then, قطا [qaṭā] Kata or katta is φάττα [phatta], that is, the wood pigeon, and it is not named from its call, as the Arabs imagine. The same judgement applies to ساق حر [sāq ḥurr] sako horrin. For ساق [sāq] sako by itself is the male of the dove. And ساق حر [sāq ḥurr] sako horrin is the male of the dove of liberty, or of the free dove, that is, of the wood pigeon, or also of the turtledove, as some hold. For like the Hebrew דרור deror, so the Arabic حر [ḥurr] horro means free. And the root حر [ḥarra], in Syriac and Chaldee חרר harar, means to be free and to grant freedom. Therefore, whenever דרור is taken in the sacred text for liberty, the Chaldee [col. 53] [II, 592] translators have חירות in its place, and the Arabic ones حرية [ḥurriyya]. Nor indeed is it obscure why among the Orientals wild and field doves are named from liberty. For Basil too, in Epistle 175 to Julitta, calls a flock of such doves αὐτόνομον ἀγέλην [autonomon agelēn], a free flock, living by its own laws. For in Greek αὐτόνομος [autonomos] is the same as ἐλεύθερος [eleutheros]. Hence Thucydides in book 2 calls the same peoples indiscriminately αὐτονόμους [autonomous] and ἐλευθέρους [eleutherous]. And in Plutarch, in the dialogue On the Daemon of Socrates, Epaminondas declares himself a citizen ἐλευθέρας καὶ αὐτονόμου πόλεως [eleutheras kai autonomou poleōs]. And Demosthenes, in the First Philippic, says of the peoples who were of Philip's party: αὐτονομούμενα καὶ ἐλεύθερα (ἔθνη) ὑπῆρχε [autonomoumena kai eleuthera (ethnē) hypērche]. Accordingly Isocrates opposes αὐτονομίαν [autonomian] to servitude, saying that under Evagoras the Greeks had ἀντὶ δουλείας αὐτονομίαν [anti douleias autonomian]. Therefore, following Basil, you would rightly render the Hebrew דרור deror as αὐτόνομον περιστεράν [autonomon peristeran].

In the two passages of Scripture in which דרור deror occurs for a bird, there is nothing that conflicts in the least with this interpretation. In Prov. XXVI, 2. the דרור seems to be commended for the swiftness of its flight, in which, as we have shown in its place ^{(1)}, the dove can compete with any bird whatever. And in Psal. LXXXIV, 4. the Psalmist groans, comparing his lot with the meanest birds, namely the sparrow and the דרור deror, that is, the field dove, to which not only free access to the altar of God was granted, but also to nest and hatch their young there, while he himself was a wanderer, an exile, and far from the sacred house. In the name of the altar there must be a figure of speech. For amid so great a throng of men and sacrifices, staying on the altar itself would not have been safe for birds. Therefore altar is put for the tabernacle, or for the temple: for the tabernacle if David speaks in this Psalm; for the temple if someone else after David ^{(2)}. For the Hebrews are in doubt, as one may learn from Kimchi. However that may be, both the tabernacle [II, 593] and the temple ^{b)} rested on great beams of cedar and of ἀρκευθίναις [arkeuthinais], in which kind of cedar the wood pigeon likes to nest, as these lines of Theocritus, Idyll 5, teach.
